title: Delirium vs Dementia
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Delirium is acute, fluctuating brain dysfunction and should trigger a search for reversible illness, medication effects, hypoxia, infection, pain, retention, constipation, dehydration, or metabolic problems. Dementia is usually chronic and progressive; a patient with dementia can still develop superimposed delirium.
recognize: Delirium often has abrupt onset, fluctuating attention, altered alertness, disorganized thinking, and sleep-wake disruption.
Dementia usually develops gradually with persistent cognitive decline and relatively preserved alertness until later stages.
priorities: Treat new confusion as a change in condition, not normal aging.
Assess oxygenation, glucose, vital signs, pain, medications, elimination, hydration, infection clues, and recent procedures/environmental changes.
Use calm reorientation and protect from falls while the cause is evaluated.
assessMonitor: Trend attention and level of consciousness over time, not just orientation questions.
Compare with baseline cognition using family/caregiver information when available.
interventions: Promote sleep, mobility, hydration, hearing/vision aids, familiar cues, and daytime orientation.
Avoid unnecessary restraints and sedating medications that can worsen delirium.
medicationSafety: Anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, opioids, sedative-hypnotics, and polypharmacy can contribute; review recent medication changes.
teaching: Families should report sudden changes from baseline promptly rather than assuming they are progression of dementia.
delegationScope: Observation and routine reorientation may be delegated, but new confusion requires licensed-nurse assessment and escalation.
examTrap: Labeling sudden postoperative confusion as dementia or normal aging.
oneLinePearl: Acute and fluctuating = delirium until a cause is found.
sourceBasis: National Institute on Aging delirium and dementia resources

title: Polypharmacy and Medication Safety
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
bottomLine: Older adults are more vulnerable to adverse drug effects and interactions because of multiple medications, comorbidities, and age-related changes in renal/hepatic handling. Medication reconciliation must include prescriptions, OTC drugs, vitamins, herbals, alcohol, and duplicate products.
recognize: New dizziness, falls, confusion, constipation, urinary retention, sedation, or orthostasis may be medication-related rather than a new disease.
Multiple prescribers and pharmacies increase duplication and interaction risk.
priorities: Maintain an accurate medication list with indication and dosing schedule.
Report new symptoms after medication changes.
Assess adherence barriers, swallowing difficulty, cost, cognition, vision, and dexterity.
assessMonitor: Trend renal function when relevant, blood pressure/orthostasis, sedation, falls, bleeding, glucose, electrolytes, and other medication-specific monitoring.
interventions: Use pill organizers or packaging systems only when they match the patient's cognition and regimen.
Encourage one updated medication list to be shared across clinicians and pharmacy visits.
medicationSafety: Do not independently stop chronic medications because they appear unnecessary; flag potential duplication, interaction, or high-risk adverse effects for review.
OTC sleep aids and antihistamines may contain anticholinergic drugs that increase confusion and falls.
teaching: Keep a current list of every prescription, OTC medicine, vitamin, and supplement and review it at every transition of care.
delegationScope: Medication reconciliation and evaluation of adverse effects are licensed-nurse responsibilities within scope; data collection can support but not replace assessment.
examTrap: Adding another medication for a new symptom before considering whether an existing drug caused it.
oneLinePearl: In older adults, a new symptom may be a new side effect.
sourceBasis: FDA Medication Safety Tips for Older Adults
FDA As You Age: You and Your Medicines

title: Elder Abuse and Neglect
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Possible elder abuse requires privacy, objective assessment, immediate safety evaluation, careful documentation, and reporting according to state law and setting requirements. Do not confront a suspected abuser in a way that increases danger before a safety plan is in place.
recognize: Concerning patterns include unexplained injuries, repeated delays in care, inconsistent histories, poor hygiene, pressure injuries, malnutrition, medication withholding, fearfulness around a caregiver, or unexplained financial changes.
Abuse can be physical, sexual, emotional, financial, neglectful, or abandonment.
priorities: Interview the patient privately when possible and use direct, nonjudgmental questions.
Treat urgent injuries and assess immediate danger.
Follow mandatory reporting requirements and facility safeguarding procedures.
assessMonitor: Document objective findings, exact patient statements when relevant, injury location/pattern, nutrition, cognition/capacity, medication access, and caregiver behavior.
interventions: Engage social work, Adult Protective Services, law enforcement, or long-term-care ombudsman/licensing resources as appropriate to setting and danger level.
medicationSafety: Medication misuse, over-sedation, or withholding can be forms of mistreatment; reconcile actual access and administration.
teaching: Explain that help is available and that reporting pathways vary by state and care setting.
delegationScope: Suspected abuse assessment, documentation, and mandated reporting cannot be delegated away; know the state/facility reporting pathway.
examTrap: Calling the suspected caregiver into the room to explain the injuries before interviewing the patient privately.
oneLinePearl: Private interview, objective documentation, safety first, report per law.

title: Advance Directives and Patient Wishes
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
bottomLine: An advance directive communicates future care preferences and may name a healthcare proxy. A capable patient makes their own current decisions; an advance directive becomes especially important when the patient cannot decide. The nurse must locate, communicate, and honor valid wishes through the care team rather than substituting personal values.
recognize: A living will, healthcare proxy/durable power of attorney for healthcare, and portable medical orders are related but not identical documents.
Capacity is decision-specific and can fluctuate; diagnosis alone does not automatically remove decision-making rights.
priorities: Ask whether an advance directive exists and ensure it is accessible in the record when provided.
Escalate conflicts between documented wishes, surrogate requests, and current orders.
Continue comfort and appropriate care regardless of code status.
assessMonitor: Assess current decision-making ability, patient understanding, and whether the listed surrogate is legally appropriate under state policy.
interventions: Facilitate communication with the provider, ethics resources, social work, or chaplaincy when conflict persists.
redFlags: Current orders conflict with known valid wishes
Family attempts to override a capable patient's decision
Unclear surrogate authority during urgent decisions
teaching: Encourage patients to discuss wishes with chosen decision-makers and keep documents available to the healthcare system.
delegationScope: Assessment of capacity concerns and interpretation of legal documents require licensed clinical/legal escalation; clerical scanning alone is not enough.
examTrap: Allowing family preference to override the decision of a capable adult patient.
oneLinePearl: The capable patient speaks first; documents and surrogates speak when the patient cannot.
sourceBasis: CMS patient rights and advance-directive requirements

title: Delegation: Stable, Predictable, Routine
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
bottomLine: Delegate tasks—not nursing judgment. Appropriate delegated care is generally routine, predictable, and performed for a stable patient by someone with verified competence, with clear instructions and required supervision. Scope for LPN/LVN practice varies by state.
recognize: New admissions, unstable patients, unexpected changes, initial assessments, care-plan decisions, and patient teaching that requires nursing judgment generally stay with licensed nurses at the appropriate level.
Routine ADLs, stable vital signs, ambulation, intake/output, and specimen collection may be delegable when policy permits.
priorities: Match the task to patient stability, worker competency, and legal/facility scope.
Give specific instructions including what findings must be reported immediately.
Follow up and evaluate the outcome.
assessMonitor: Reassess the patient after delegated care when the result affects the care plan or condition.
interventions: Reassign when patient acuity changes or the worker is not competent for the task.
medicationSafety: Medication administration delegation varies widely by setting and state; follow law and policy rather than a universal rule.
redFlags: Worker reports inability to complete task safely
teaching: Team members should know exactly what to report and when.
delegationScope: Use the state's nurse practice act and facility policy for LPN/LVN and UAP boundaries; never assume another state's rules apply.
examTrap: Delegating assessment of a newly confused or unstable patient because the task sounds simple.
oneLinePearl: Stable + routine + competent worker + clear follow-up = delegation candidate.
sourceBasis: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation

title: Incident Reports and Just Culture
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: After an error, fall, equipment failure, or near miss, care for the patient first, notify the appropriate clinician, document objective clinical facts in the health record, and complete the organization’s safety report separately. Do not chart that an incident report was filed unless policy specifically requires it.
recognize: Near misses matter because they reveal system hazards even when no injury occurred.
The safety report is for quality/risk processes and does not replace the clinical record.
priorities: Assess and stabilize the patient.
Notify the RN/provider and other required parties.
Document the event's clinical facts, assessments, interventions, and patient response objectively.
assessMonitor: Trend for delayed effects of medication errors, falls, exposure events, or equipment failures.
interventions: Preserve relevant equipment or medication packaging when instructed by policy.
Participate in factual review without altering the record to hide an error.
medicationSafety: Medication-error response depends on the drug, dose, route, time, and patient condition; assess toxicity risk rather than applying one generic action.
redFlags: Any error with possible life-threatening effect
teaching: Explain patient care and follow-up honestly according to organizational disclosure policy and the care team's process.
delegationScope: A nurse who identifies an event remains responsible for immediate patient safety and required reporting; do not delegate away the response.
examTrap: Completing the incident report before assessing the patient.
oneLinePearl: Patient first, facts in chart, safety report separate.
sourceBasis: The Joint Commission patient safety event principles

title: Newborn Thermoregulation
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: Newborns lose heat easily through evaporation, conduction, convection, and radiation. Prevent cold stress with prompt drying, skin-to-skin contact when stable, warm blankets/hat, environmental control, and delayed bathing until temperature is stable.
recognize: Cold stress increases oxygen and glucose consumption and can contribute to hypoglycemia and respiratory distress.
Preterm and low-birth-weight infants have especially limited temperature control.
priorities: Dry wet skin immediately after birth and remove wet linens.
Use skin-to-skin contact and warm covering for stable infants.
Rewarm gradually and assess glucose/respiratory status when hypothermia is significant or persistent.
assessMonitor: Trend axillary temperature per unit practice, respiratory effort, feeding, glucose when indicated, and environmental exposures.
interventions: Use prewarmed surfaces and avoid placing the bassinet near cold windows, vents, or air currents.
teaching: Teach safe skin-to-skin warming and appropriate clothing without overheating or unsafe sleep practices.
delegationScope: Routine temperature collection may be delegated according to policy, but abnormal newborn temperature requires licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Bathing a newly born infant before temperature is stable.
oneLinePearl: Dry, skin-to-skin, cover—cold babies burn glucose and oxygen.
sourceBasis: American Academy of Pediatrics newborn care guidance

title: Newborn Jaundice and Hyperbilirubinemia
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Jaundice must be interpreted by the newborn's age in hours, gestational age, bilirubin level, feeding, and neurotoxicity risk factors. Jaundice in the first 24 hours, rapidly rising bilirubin, poor feeding, lethargy, abnormal tone, or a level near treatment thresholds requires prompt evaluation.
recognize: Visible jaundice alone cannot accurately quantify bilirubin.
The AAP recommends bilirubin measurement before discharge and follow-up based on the bilirubin's distance from the age-specific phototherapy threshold.
priorities: Assess feeding effectiveness, output, weight change, gestational age, bruising/cephalohematoma, blood-group incompatibility risk, and jaundice onset.
Obtain transcutaneous or serum bilirubin as ordered and interpret using the current AAP pathway.
Promote effective feeding and timely follow-up.
assessMonitor: Trend bilirubin, weight, intake, urine/stool output, hydration, alertness, tone, and feeding quality.
interventions: During phototherapy, maximize prescribed light exposure while protecting eyes according to device protocol and maintaining hydration/feeding.
Do not rely on sunlight as treatment for significant hyperbilirubinemia.
teaching: Teach parents to keep follow-up appointments and seek care for worsening jaundice, poor feeding, fewer wet diapers, extreme sleepiness, or abnormal movements.
delegationScope: Routine feeding/output data can be delegated, but bilirubin-risk interpretation and abnormal neurologic findings require licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Reassuring parents based only on the skin color without considering age in hours or bilirubin measurement.
oneLinePearl: Newborn bilirubin is always an age-in-hours problem.
sourceBasis: American Academy of Pediatrics 2022 Hyperbilirubinemia Clinical Practice Guideline, valid through 2027

title: Neonatal Hypoglycemia
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Newborn hypoglycemia may be asymptomatic or present with jitteriness, poor feeding, lethargy, apnea, cyanosis, temperature instability, or seizures. Screen infants with established risk factors according to protocol, feed early when appropriate, and treat symptomatic or persistent low glucose promptly.
recognize: Risk is increased in infants of diabetic mothers, small- or large-for-gestational-age infants, preterm infants, and infants with illness or cold stress.
Jitteriness can have other causes, so glucose should be checked when indicated rather than assumed.
priorities: Maintain warmth and initiate feeding early for stable at-risk infants according to protocol.
Check glucose at protocol-defined times and confirm/treat low values as directed.
Symptomatic infants or severe/persistent hypoglycemia require rapid escalation and IV dextrose when ordered.
assessMonitor: Trend glucose, feeding, temperature, respiratory status, neurologic behavior, and recurrence after treatment.
interventions: Support breastfeeding or expressed milk/formula supplementation according to the individualized feeding plan.
Oral dextrose gel may be used in some newborn protocols for appropriate infants.
medicationSafety: IV dextrose requires careful concentration/rate management and glucose reassessment to avoid recurrence or excessive shifts.
teaching: Teach parents feeding frequency and warning signs before discharge when the infant has had glucose instability.
delegationScope: Point-of-care glucose collection may be delegated when policy allows; abnormal results and symptoms require licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Putting a jittery at-risk newborn under a warmer and waiting without checking glucose.
oneLinePearl: Warmth, feeding, glucose—jittery newborns need a number.
sourceBasis: American Academy of Pediatrics newborn glucose guidance

title: Postpartum Depression vs Postpartum Psychosis
bottomLine: Persistent depression, anxiety, loss of interest, guilt, hopelessness, or impaired functioning postpartum requires evaluation for perinatal depression. Delusions, hallucinations, severe confusion, mania, or thoughts of harming self or infant suggest postpartum psychosis and require emergency psychiatric intervention and infant safety planning.
recognize: Brief tearfulness and emotional lability in the first days can be postpartum blues, but symptoms that persist, worsen, or impair function need further evaluation.
Postpartum psychosis often begins abruptly and may include bizarre beliefs about the infant or severe insomnia/mania.
priorities: Ask directly about suicidal thoughts, self-harm, thoughts of harming the infant, psychotic symptoms, and ability to provide safe care.
Do not leave a patient with active dangerous thoughts or psychosis alone with the infant.
Activate emergency psychiatric and obstetric support for psychosis or imminent risk.
assessMonitor: Assess sleep, support system, prior bipolar/psychotic history, substance use, functioning, bonding, safety, and treatment adherence.
interventions: Connect patients with perinatal mental-health treatment and practical support.
Use nonjudgmental language to reduce shame and encourage disclosure.
medicationSafety: Medication choice during lactation requires individualized risk-benefit review; do not tell patients to abruptly stop psychiatric medication without prescriber guidance.
teaching: Perinatal mood disorders are medical conditions; urgent help is required for psychosis or safety concerns.
delegationScope: Safety assessment for suicide, psychosis, or infant harm is a licensed clinical responsibility and requires immediate escalation.
examTrap: Calling hallucinations or bizarre beliefs normal postpartum adjustment.
oneLinePearl: Depression needs treatment; psychosis needs emergency protection.
sourceBasis: ACOG Clinical Practice Guideline: Treatment and Management of Mental Health Conditions During Pregnancy and Postpartum
ACOG Perinatal Mental Health Screening Guidance
